passages.title: Waardenburg syndrome type 3: overview
passages.text: Waardenburg syndrome type 3 (ORPHA:896; MONDO:0007862). Also known as Klein-Waardenburg syndrome, WS3, Waardenburg syndrome type III, Waardenburg syndrome with limb anomalies, Waardenburg syndrome with upper limb anomalies. Waardenburg syndrome type 3 (WS3) is a very rare subtype of Waardenburg syndrome (WS) that is characterized by limb anomalies in association with congenital hearing loss, minor defects in structures arising from neural crest, resulting in pigmentation anomalies of eyes, hair, and skin. Associated genes: PAX3. The HPO annotates 22 phenotypic features for this disease.

sentences.text: Leading candidates for 14 recorded features and 2 recorded absences.
1. Waardenburg syndrome, type 3 (OMIM:148820), estimated probability 57% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Bilateral wrist flexion contracture; Partial albinism; White eyelashes; White eyebrow.
Recorded absent but typical: Axillary pterygium (1 of 2 reported patients); Upper limb amyotrophy (1 of 2 reported patients).
Worth checking: Premature graying of hair; White forelock; Heterochromia iridis.
2. Oculocutaneous albinism type 2 (ORPHA:79432), estimated probability 4% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: White eyebrow; Blue irides; White eyelashes; Partial albinism (annotated as Hypopigmentation of the skin).
Worth checking: Macular hypopigmentation; Optic nerve misrouting; White hair.
3. Simosa craniofacial syndrome (OMIM:182150), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Telecanthus; Posteriorly rotated ears; White eyebrow (annotated as Highly arched eyebrow); White eyelashes (annotated as Abnormal hair morphology).
Worth checking: Depressed nasal tip; Long nose; Hypernasal speech.
4. Blepharophimosis, epicanthus inversus, and ptosis (OMIM:110100), estimated probability 2% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Epicanthus inversus; Telecanthus; Short palpebral fissure (annotated as Blepharophimosis).
Worth checking: Narrow palpebral fissure; Blepharophimosis; Sparse pubic hair.
5. Parenti-Mignot neurodevelopmental syndrome (OMIM:619873), estimated probability 2% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Prominent nasal tip; Prominent nasal bridge; Delayed fine motor development (annotated as Motor delay); Posteriorly rotated ears.
Worth checking: Craniosynostosis.
The most informative next question is whether highly arched eyebrow is present: present favours Simosa craniofacial syndrome, absent favours Waardenburg syndrome, type 3.

Genes behind the leading candidates, in order: PAX3 (Waardenburg syndrome, type 3); MC1R (Oculocutaneous albinism type 2); OCA2 (Oculocutaneous albinism type 2); FOXL2 (Blepharophimosis, epicanthus inversus, and ptosis); CHD5 (Parenti-Mignot neurodevelopmental syndrome).
This is decision support for a clinical geneticist: any diagnosis needs genetic testing and specialist review.

sources.DIS|OMIM:182150|overview: Simosa craniofacial syndrome: overview. Simosa craniofacial syndrome (OMIM:182150; MONDO:0008421). Also known as Simosa-Penchaszadeh-Bustos syndrome, blepharophimosis-telecanthus-microstomia syndrome. Flat face-microstomia-ear anomaly syndrome is a rare, genetic, multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by dysmorphic facial features, including high forehead, elongated and flattened midface, arched and sparse eyebrows, short palpebral fissures, telecanthus, long nose with hypoplastic nostrils, long philtrum, high and narrow palate and microstomia with downturned corners. Ears are characteristically malformed, large, low-set and posteriorly rotated and nasal speech is associated. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1994. Mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant inheritance. The HPO annotates 24 phenotypic features for this disease.

passages.title: Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type 1: overview
passages.text: Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type 1 (ORPHA:77258; MONDO:0008596). Also known as Sugio-Kajii syndrome, TRPS 1, TRPS1, trichorhinophalangeal dysplasia (syndrome) types 1/3, trichorhinophalangeal dysplasia type I, trichorhinophalangeal dysplasia types 1/3, trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type I, trichorhinophalangeal syndrome, type 1, and 2 more. An autosomal dominant malformation syndrome caused by mutations in TRPS1 characterized by distinctive craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities. TRPS I patients have sparse scalp hair, bulbous tip of the nose, long flat philtrum, thin upper vermilion border, and protruding ears. Skeletal abnormalities include cone-shaped epiphyses at the phalanges, hip malformations, and short stature. Associated genes: TRPS1. The HPO annotates 29 phenotypic features for this disease.

sources.DIS|OMIM:190350|overview: Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome, type I: overview. Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome, type I (OMIM:190350; MONDO:0008596). Also known as Sugio-Kajii syndrome, TRPS 1, TRPS1, trichorhinophalangeal dysplasia (syndrome) types 1/3, trichorhinophalangeal dysplasia type I, trichorhinophalangeal dysplasia types 1/3, trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type 1, trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type I, and 2 more. An autosomal dominant malformation syndrome caused by mutations in TRPS1 characterized by distinctive craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities. TRPS I patients have sparse scalp hair, bulbous tip of the nose, long flat philtrum, thin upper vermilion border, and protruding ears. Skeletal abnormalities include cone-shaped epiphyses at the phalanges, hip malformations, and short stature. Mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant inheritance. Associated genes: TRPS1. The HPO annotates 53 phenotypic features for this disease.

sources.DIS|OMIM:182150|overview: Simosa craniofacial syndrome: overview. Simosa craniofacial syndrome (OMIM:182150; MONDO:0008421). Also known as Simosa-Penchaszadeh-Bustos syndrome, blepharophimosis-telecanthus-microstomia syndrome. Flat face-microstomia-ear anomaly syndrome is a rare, genetic, multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by dysmorphic facial features, including high forehead, elongated and flattened midface, arched and sparse eyebrows, short palpebral fissures, telecanthus, long nose with hypoplastic nostrils, long philtrum, high and narrow palate and microstomia with downturned corners. Ears are characteristically malformed, large, low-set and posteriorly rotated and nasal speech is associated. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1994. Mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant inheritance. The HPO annotates 24 phenotypic features for this disease.

passages.text: Mild fetal ventriculomegaly (HP:0010952). A kind of ventriculomegaly occurring in the fetal period and usually diagnosed by prenatal ultrasound. Cerebral ventriculomegaly is defined by atrial measurements 10 mm or more. Mild ventriculomegaly (MVM) is defined as measurements between 10 and 15 mm. Measurements are obtained from an axial plane at the level of the thalamic nuclei just below the standard image to measure the BPD (PMID:16100637). Synonyms: Mild foetal ventriculomegaly. Worth checking: Myelopathy; Elevated brain choline level by MRS; Cerebellar edema.
3. Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1-alpha deficiency (ORPHA:79243), estimated probability 2% among the shortlisted candidates.

Supporting features: Increased circulating lactate concentration; Periventricular cysts (annotated as Periventricular leukomalacia); Ventriculomegaly; Cerebellar atrophy (annotated as Cerebellar cyst).
Recorded absent but typical: Seizure (frequent (30 to 79%)); Small for gestational age (very frequent (80 to 99%)); Cerebral atrophy (frequent (30 to 79%)).
Worth checking: Abnormal CSF pyruvate family amino acid concentration; Abnormal medullary pyramid morphology; Congenital lactic acidosis.
4. Neurodevelopmental disorder with structural brain abnormalities and craniofacial abnormalities (OMIM:621393), estimated probability 2% among the shortlisted candidates.

Supporting features: Global brain atrophy; Periventricular cysts (annotated as Abnormal periventricular white matter morphology); Cerebellar atrophy (annotated as Cerebellar vermis atrophy); Ventriculomegaly.
Recorded absent but typical: Microcephaly (3 of 5 reported patients); Micrognathia (4 of 5 reported patients); Thin corpus callosum (4 of 5 reported patients).
Worth checking: Fetal skin edema; Enlarged fetal cisterna magna; Brainstem dysplasia.
5. Parkinsonism-dystonia 3, childhood-onset (OMIM:619738), estimated probability 2% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Global brain atrophy; Premature birth; Cerebellar atrophy.
Worth checking: Stooped posture; Expressive language delay; Hyperkinetic movements.

passages.title: Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 76: overview
passages.text: Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 76 (ORPHA:488594; MONDO:0014827). Also known as CAPN1 autosomal recessive complex spastic paraplegia, SPG76, autosomal recessive complex spastic paraplegia caused by mutation in CAPN1, hereditary spastic paraplegia type 76, spastic paraplegia 76, autosomal recessive. Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 76 is a rare, complex hereditary spastic paraplegia characterized by adult onset slowly progressive, mild to moderate lower limb spasticity and hyperreflexia, resulting in gait disturbances, commonly associated with upper limb hyperreflexia and dysarthria. Foot deformities (usually pes cavus) and extensor plantar responses are also frequent. Additional features may include ataxia, lower limb weakness/amyotrophy, abnormal bladder function, distal sensory loss and mild intellectual deterioration. Associated genes: CAPN1. The HPO annotates 17 phenotypic features for this disease.

1. Spastic paraplegia 76, autosomal recessive (OMIM:616907), estimated probability 19% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Gait imbalance; Lower limb hyperreflexia; Ankle clonus; Loss of ambulation.
Worth checking: Upper limb hyperreflexia; Lower limb muscle weakness; Pes cavus.
2. Spastic ataxia 10, autosomal recessive (OMIM:620666), estimated probability 16% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Ankle clonus; Lower limb hyperreflexia; Loss of ambulation; Babinski sign.
Worth checking: Knee clonus; Hoffmann sign; Postural instability.
3. Spastic ataxia 11, autosomal dominant (OMIM:621226), estimated probability 5% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Ankle clonus; Lower limb hyperreflexia (annotated as Hyperactive patellar reflex); Babinski sign; Cerebellar atrophy.
Worth checking: Abnormal motor evoked potentials; Abnormality of somatosensory evoked potentials; Lower limb hypertonia.
4. Neurodevelopmental disorder with regression, abnormal movements, loss of speech, and seizures (OMIM:618088), estimated probability 5% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Loss of ambulation; Dysarthria; Babinski sign; Cerebellar atrophy.
Worth checking: Loss of speech; Absent speech; Developmental regression.
5. Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 5A (ORPHA:100986), estimated probability 5% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Ankle clonus; Babinski sign; Appendicular spasticity (annotated as Spastic paraplegia); Cerebellar atrophy (annotated as Abnormal cerebellum morphology).
Worth checking: Impaired vibratory sensation; Lower limb muscle weakness; Lower limb amyotrophy.
The most informative next question is whether spastic paraplegia is present: present favours Spastic paraplegia 76, autosomal recessive, absent favours Spastic ataxia 10, autosomal recessive.

Genes behind the leading candidates, in order: CAPN1 (Spastic paraplegia 76, autosomal recessive); COQ4 (Spastic ataxia 10, autosomal recessive); TUBA4A (Spastic ataxia 11, autosomal dominant); IRF2BPL (Neurodevelopmental disorder with regression, abnormal movements, loss of speech, and seizures); CYP7B1 (Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 5A).

sentences.text: Leading candidates for 12 recorded features and 9 recorded absences.
1. Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor abnormalities, seizures, and facial dysmorphism (OMIM:620719), estimated probability 18% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Almond-shaped palpebral fissure; Narrow forehead; Status epilepticus; Axial hypotonia.
Recorded absent but typical: Epicanthus (2 of 5 reported patients); Pointed chin (2 of 5 reported patients); Sloping forehead (2 of 5 reported patients).
Worth checking: Appendicular hypotonia; Short middle phalanx of the 5th finger; Stereotypical hand wringing.
2. Van Maldergem syndrome 1 (OMIM:601390), estimated probability 5% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Narrow forehead; Wide nasal bridge; Ptosis; High palate.
Recorded absent but typical: Epicanthus.
Worth checking: Periventricular nodular heterotopia; Radial head subluxation; Wide anterior fontanel.
3. Agenesis of the corpus callosum with peripheral neuropathy (OMIM:218000), estimated probability 5% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Narrow forehead; Thin corpus callosum (annotated as Agenesis of corpus callosum); Wide nasal bridge; Ptosis.
Worth checking: Increased CSF protein concentration; Axonal degeneration/regeneration; Decreased nerve conduction velocity.
4. Xia-Gibbs syndrome (OMIM:615829), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Almond-shaped palpebral fissure; Thin corpus callosum (annotated as Agenesis of corpus callosum); Narrow forehead; High palate.
Recorded absent but typical: Epicanthus (2 of 2 reported patients); Intrauterine growth retardation (1 of 1 reported patients); Cerebral atrophy (4 of 4 reported patients).
Worth checking: Narrow nail; Impaired toileting ability; Abnormality of the cochlear nerve.
5. Intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal recessive 35 (OMIM:615162), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Low-set ears; Hypertelorism; Global developmental delay; Intellectual disability.
Worth checking: Thick nasal alae; Hypoplasia of the ulna; Flat occiput.

The most informative next question is whether hyporeflexia is present: present favours Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor abnormalities, seizures, and facial dysmorphism, absent favours Van Maldergem syndrome 1.

Genes behind the leading candidates, in order: PUM1 (Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor abnormalities, seizures, and facial dysmorphism); DCHS1 (Van Maldergem syndrome 1); SLC12A6 (Agenesis of the corpus callosum with peripheral neuropathy); AHDC1 (Xia-Gibbs syndrome); CDK10 (Al Kaissi syndrome).
This is decision support for a clinical geneticist: any diagnosis needs genetic testing and specialist review.

sentences.text: Leading candidates for 6 recorded features and 5 recorded absences.
1. Spastic ataxia 10, autosomal recessive (OMIM:620666), estimated probability 28% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Lower limb hyperreflexia; Limb ataxia; Lower limb spasticity; Gait ataxia.
Recorded absent but typical: Babinski sign (10 of 16 reported patients); Upper limb hyperreflexia (4 of 9 reported patients).
Worth checking: Knee clonus; Hoffmann sign; Ankle clonus.
2. Spastic paraplegia 7, autosomal recessive (OMIM:607259), estimated probability 7% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Lower limb hyperreflexia; Limb ataxia; Lower limb spasticity (annotated as Spastic paraplegia); Gait ataxia.
Recorded absent but typical: Cerebellar atrophy (41 of 43 reported patients); Babinski sign (22 of 42 reported patients).
Worth checking: Impaired executive functioning; Lower limb hypertonia; Spastic ataxia.
3. Spinocerebellar ataxia type 28 (ORPHA:101109), estimated probability 6% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Limb ataxia; Lower limb hyperreflexia; Gait ataxia; Dysarthria.
Recorded absent but typical: Babinski sign (frequent (30 to 79%)).
Worth checking: Slow saccadic eye movements; Ophthalmoparesis.
4. Spastic paraplegia 76, autosomal recessive (OMIM:616907), estimated probability 2% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Limb ataxia; Lower limb hyperreflexia; Lower limb spasticity (annotated as Spastic paraplegia); Gait ataxia.
Recorded absent but typical: Cerebellar atrophy (1 of 1 reported patients); Babinski sign (8 of 10 reported patients); Upper limb spasticity (3 of 4 reported patients).
Worth checking: Spastic ataxia; Gait imbalance; Loss of ambulation.
5. Spastic paraplegia 92, autosomal recessive (OMIM:620911), estimated probability 2% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Limb ataxia; Lower limb hyperreflexia; Lower limb spasticity (annotated as Spastic paraparesis); Gait ataxia.
Recorded absent but typical: Postural tremor (1 of 1 reported patients); Babinski sign (4 of 5 reported patients); Upper limb spasticity (2 of 5 reported patients).
Worth checking: Impaired distal vibration sensation; Lower limb muscle weakness; Intention tremor.
The most informative next question is whether knee clonus is present: present favours Spastic ataxia 10, autosomal recessive, absent favours Spastic ataxia 10, autosomal recessive.

Genes behind the leading candidates, in order: COQ4 (Spastic ataxia 10, autosomal recessive); SPG7 (Spastic paraplegia 7, autosomal recessive); AFG3L2 (Spinocerebellar ataxia type 28); CAPN1 (Spastic paraplegia 76, autosomal recessive); STUB1 (Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia due to STUB1 deficiency).

Supporting features: Increased circulating lactate concentration; Respiratory insufficiency (annotated as Respiratory failure); Decreased level of coenzyme Q10 in skeletal muscle (annotated as Hepatic steatosis); Seizure.
Worth checking: Hyperglycinemia; Disseminated intravascular coagulation; Elevated circulating alanine aminotransferase concentration.
4. Coenzyme Q10 deficiency, primary, 4 (OMIM:612016), estimated probability 4% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Decreased level of coenzyme Q10 in skeletal muscle; Increased circulating lactate concentration; Seizure.
Worth checking: Increased intramyocellular lipid droplets; Elevated lactate:pyruvate ratio; Increased CSF lactate.
5. Mitochondrial myopathy with reversible cytochrome C oxidase deficiency (ORPHA:254864), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.

Supporting features: Decreased level of coenzyme Q10 in skeletal muscle (annotated as Increased muscle glycogen content); Respiratory insufficiency (annotated as Respiratory failure requiring assisted ventilation); Mitochondrial swelling (annotated as Decreased circulating carnitine concentration).

sources.DIS|OMIM:218000|overview: Agenesis of the corpus callosum with peripheral neuropathy: overview. Agenesis of the corpus callosum with peripheral neuropathy (OMIM:218000; MONDO:0000902). Also known as Andermann syndrome, Charlevoix disease, corpus callosum agenesis-neuronopathy syndrome, hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with agenesis of the corpus callosum, peripheral neuropathy associated with agenesis of the corpus callosum. Corpus callosum agenesis-neuropathy is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by severe progressive sensorimotor neuropathy beginning in infancy with resulting hypotonia, areflexia, amyotrophy and variable degrees of dysgenesis of the corpus callosum. Additional features include mild-to-severe intellectual and developmental delays, and psychiatric manifestations that include paranoid delusions, depression, hallucinations, and "autistic-like" features. Affected individuals are usually wheelchair restricted in the second decade of life and die in the third decade of life. The disease is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive inheritance. Onset: neonatal onset, progressive. Associated genes: SLC12A6. The HPO annotates 54 phenotypic features for this disease.

passages.title: Loeys-Dietz syndrome 1: overview
passages.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome 1 (OMIM:609192; MONDO:0012212). Also known as Furlong syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome caused by mutation in TGFBR1, Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 1, TGFBR1 Loeys-Dietz syndrome. A rare autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutations in the TGFBR1 gene. It is characterized by vascular abnormalities (aortic and arterial aneurysms, aortic dissection, and tortuosity of the arteries), hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and early fusion of the skull bones. Mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant inheritance. Onset: adult onset, congenital onset. Associated genes: TGFBR1. The HPO annotates 65 phenotypic features for this disease.

sentences.text: Leading candidates for 12 recorded features and 25 recorded absences.
1. Loeys-Dietz syndrome 1 (OMIM:609192), estimated probability 38% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Cervical spine instability; Dilatation of the cerebral artery; Arterial tortuosity; Bifid uvula.
Recorded absent but typical: Inguinal hernia (2 of 2 reported patients); High palate (3 of 4 reported patients); Malar flattening (23 of 38 reported patients).
Worth checking: Aortic root aneurysm; Dural ectasia; Hypoplasia of the musculature.
2. Loeys-Dietz syndrome 3 (OMIM:613795), estimated probability 30% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Arterial tortuosity (annotated as Tortuous cerebral arteries); Dilatation of the cerebral artery; Cervical spine instability; Disproportionate tall stature.
Recorded absent but typical: Inguinal hernia (12 of 39 reported patients); High palate (12 of 28 reported patients); Malar flattening (17 of 49 reported patients).
Worth checking: Intervertebral disk degeneration; Osteochondritis dissecans; Uterine prolapse.
3. Loeys-Dietz syndrome 6 (OMIM:619656), estimated probability 5% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Arterial tortuosity; Dilatation of the cerebral artery; Disproportionate tall stature; Arachnodactyly.
Recorded absent but typical: Inguinal hernia (5 of 11 reported patients); High palate (6 of 16 reported patients); Bruising susceptibility (5 of 9 reported patients).
Worth checking: Intervertebral disk degeneration; Bicuspid aortic valve; Thoracic aortic aneurysm.
4. Loeys-Dietz syndrome 5 (OMIM:615582), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Cervical spine instability; Bifid uvula; Arachnodactyly; Disproportionate tall stature (annotated as Tall stature).
Recorded absent but typical: Cleft palate (1 of 1 reported patients); Blue sclerae (1 of 1 reported patients); Pectus carinatum.
Worth checking: Bilateral coxa valga; Overhanging nasal tip; Congenital finger flexion contractures.
5. FLNA-related X-linked myxomatous valvular dysplasia (ORPHA:555877), estimated probability 2% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Mitral regurgitation; Mitral valve prolapse; Joint hypermobility.
Worth checking: Pulmonic regurgitation; Tricuspid regurgitation; Aortic regurgitation.
The most informative next question is whether hypoplasia of the musculature is present: present favours Loeys-Dietz syndrome 1, absent favours Loeys-Dietz syndrome 3.

Genes behind the leading candidates, in order: TGFBR1 (Loeys-Dietz syndrome 1); SMAD3 (Loeys-Dietz syndrome 3); SMAD2 (Loeys-Dietz syndrome 6); TGFB3 (Loeys-Dietz syndrome 5); TGFB2 (Loeys-Dietz syndrome 4).

sources.DIS|OMIM:615582|overview: Loeys-Dietz syndrome 5: overview. Loeys-Dietz syndrome 5 (OMIM:615582; MONDO:0014262). Also known as Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 5, Rienhoff syndrome. Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 (LDS5), also known as Rienhoff (pronounced REENhoff) syndrome, is characterized by syndromic presentation of aortic aneurysms involving the thoracic and/or abdominal aorta, with risk of dissection and rupture. Other systemic features include cleft palate, bifid uvula, mitral valve disease, skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine instability, and clubfoot deformity; however, not all clinical features occur in all patients. In contrast to other forms of LDS, no striking aortic or arterial tortuosity is present in these patients, and there is no strong evidence for early aortic dissection. Mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant inheritance. Associated genes: TGFB3. The HPO annotates 57 phenotypic features for this disease.

sentences.text: Leading candidates for 13 recorded features and 16 recorded absences.
1. Sotos syndrome (OMIM:117550), estimated probability 12% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Neonatal hypoglycemia; Moderate intellectual disability; Narrow palate; Atrial septal defect.
Recorded absent but typical: Hearing impairment (1 of 1 reported patients); Strabismus (1 of 1 reported patients); Nystagmus.
Worth checking: Excessive dental attrition; Fractured carpal bone; Narrow jaw.
2. Al Kaissi syndrome (OMIM:617694), estimated probability 9% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Narrow palate (annotated as High, narrow palate); Joint hypermobility; Motor delay (annotated as Delayed ability to walk); Delayed speech and language development.
Worth checking: Broad nasal tip; Small hand; Postnatal growth retardation.
3. Xia-Gibbs syndrome (OMIM:615829), estimated probability 5% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Prominent fingertip pads; Moderate intellectual disability; Joint hypermobility; Hypertrichosis (annotated as Synophrys).
Recorded absent but typical: Hearing impairment (3 of 8 reported patients); Strabismus (11 of 25 reported patients); Ptosis (14 of 41 reported patients).
Worth checking: Narrow nail; Impaired toileting ability; Abnormality of the cochlear nerve.
4. Intellectual disability-coarse face-macrocephaly-cerebellar hypotrophy syndrome (ORPHA:397709), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.

Supporting features: Motor delay (annotated as Delayed gross motor development); Abnormal facial shape (annotated as Coarse facial features); Delayed speech and language development; Hypertrichosis (annotated as Facial hypertrichosis).
Recorded absent but typical: Hearing impairment (frequent (30 to 79%)); Nystagmus (frequent (30 to 79%)); Severe intellectual disability (very frequent (80 to 99%)).
Worth checking: Severe global developmental delay; Palpebral edema; Relative macrocephaly.
5. Koolen-De Vries syndrome (OMIM:610443), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Prominent fingertip pads; Narrow palate; Joint hypermobility; Atrial septal defect.
Recorded absent but typical: Strabismus (10 of 22 reported patients); Ptosis (11 of 22 reported patients); Pulmonic stenosis.
Worth checking: Conspicuously happy disposition; Pear-shaped nose; Bulbous nose.
The most informative next question is whether excessive dental attrition is present: present favours Sotos syndrome, absent favours Al Kaissi syndrome.

Genes behind the leading candidates, in order: APC2 (Sotos syndrome); NSD1 (Sotos syndrome); CDK10 (Al Kaissi syndrome); AHDC1 (Xia-Gibbs syndrome); SNX14 (Intellectual disability-coarse face-macrocephaly-cerebellar hypotrophy syndrome).
This is decision support for a clinical geneticist: any diagnosis needs genetic testing and specialist review.
Sotos syndrome: mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant inheritance.

sentences.text: Leading candidates for 8 recorded features and 56 recorded absences.
1. GAPO syndrome (ORPHA:2067), estimated probability 5% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Broad forehead; Sparse eyebrow; High forehead; Hypertelorism.
Recorded absent but typical: Everted lower lip vermilion (very frequent (80 to 99%)); Long philtrum (very frequent (80 to 99%)); Low-set ears (very frequent (80 to 99%)).
Worth checking: Early balding; Thick nasal alae; Underdeveloped supraorbital ridges.
2. Xia-Gibbs syndrome (OMIM:615829), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Exodeviation (annotated as Exotropia); High forehead; Broad forehead; Thin upper lip vermilion.
Recorded absent but typical: Abnormality of the genital system (1 of 2 reported patients); Cleft palate (1 of 4 reported patients); High palate (6 of 14 reported patients).
Worth checking: Narrow nail; Impaired toileting ability; Abnormality of the cochlear nerve.
3. Neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired language, behavioral abnormalities, and dysmorphic facies (OMIM:620494), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: Exodeviation (annotated as Exotropia); Round face; Broad forehead; Thin upper lip vermilion.
Recorded absent but typical: High palate (2 of 2 reported patients); Everted lower lip vermilion (2 of 2 reported patients); Epicanthus (2 of 2 reported patients).
Worth checking: Thumb symphalangism; Increased femoral anteversion; Anhydramnios.
4. Intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (OMIM:618089), estimated probability 3% among the shortlisted candidates.
Supporting features: High forehead; Exodeviation (annotated as Strabismus); Sparse eyebrow; Broad forehead.
Recorded absent but typical: Posteriorly rotated ears; Deeply set eye; Microtia.
